title: Context-Free Grammars
body:
A set of rewrite rules that **generates** a language, rather than a machine that recognises
one. This is the generative half of the second rung of the ladder; [[Pushdown Automata]] are
the recognising half, and they cover the same class.

## Formal definition

A 4-tuple $G = (V, \Sigma, R, S)$:

| Part | What it is |
|---|---|
| $V$ | finite set of **variables** (non-terminals), written in capitals |
| $\Sigma$ | finite set of **terminals**, the actual [[Alphabet]], disjoint from $V$ |
| $R$ | rules of the form $A \to \alpha$ where $A \in V$ and $\alpha \in (V \cup \Sigma)^*$ |
| $S \in V$ | start variable |

**Context-free** means the left side of every rule is a single variable. You may replace $A$
with its body no matter what surrounds it, and the context never gets a vote. Allow strings on
the left and you move up to context-sensitive grammars and out of this part of the course.

## Derivation

Start at $S$, repeatedly replace one variable with the right-hand side of one of its rules,
stop when only terminals remain. $L(G)$ is the set of terminal strings you can reach.

$$S \to aSb \mid \varepsilon$$

```
S => aSb => aaSbb => aaaSbbb => aaabbb
```

That generates $\{a^n b^n\}$, the language the [[Pumping Lemma]] proved is not regular. One
recursive rule buys you the counting a [[DFA]] cannot do, because the recursion stacks the
`a`s and the `b`s against each other automatically.

Balanced brackets, same shape:

$$S \to (S) \mid SS \mid \varepsilon$$

## Parse trees and ambiguity

A **parse tree** is a derivation drawn as a [[Tree]]: root $S$, internal nodes variables,
leaves the terminals read left to right. It is the structure, with the order of replacements
thrown away.

A grammar is **ambiguous** if some string has two different parse trees. The classic:

$$E \to E + E \mid E \times E \mid \text{num}$$

`1 + 2 * 3` parses two ways, and they compute different numbers. The fix is to encode
precedence in the grammar with extra layers:

$$E \to E + T \mid T \qquad T \to T \times F \mid F \qquad F \to \text{num} \mid (E)$$

Now there is exactly one tree, and it is the one that binds $\times$ tighter. Some languages
are **inherently ambiguous**: no unambiguous grammar exists for them at all. Checking whether
an arbitrary grammar is ambiguous is [[Undecidability|undecidable]].

Related pathology: the [[Dangling else]] problem, where `if a then if b then x else y` has two
readings. Real languages patch it by fiat, matching `else` to the nearest `if`.

## Chomsky Normal Form

Every CFG can be converted so that every rule is $A \to BC$ or $A \to a$, plus
$S \to \varepsilon$ if needed. It makes proofs and parsing algorithms simpler: every parse tree
becomes binary, so a derivation of a length-$n$ string takes exactly $2n - 1$ steps. This is
what the CYK parsing algorithm requires.

## Why it matters outside the theory

Programming language **syntax is context-free**, and that is not a coincidence: nesting is what
grammars do and what [[Regular Expressions]] cannot. Every compiler front end is a lexer
(regular, a [[DFA]]) feeding a parser (context-free, a [[Stack]] machine). Which is exactly
the two bottom rungs of this course, shipped.

The things a CFG cannot check are the things compilers report *after* parsing: variables
declared before use, argument counts, type agreement. Those need context, so they land in the
semantic pass. Written in BNF, the rule notation above is the same thing every language
specification uses to define its syntax.

## Core Facts to Know

- A CFG is $(V, \Sigma, R, S)$: variables, terminals, rules, start variable.
- Context-free means every rule has exactly one variable on the left.
- $L(G)$ is the set of terminal strings derivable from $S$.
- CFGs and [[Pushdown Automata]] recognise exactly the same class: the context-free languages.
- Every regular language is context-free; the reverse is false.
- $S \to aSb \mid \varepsilon$ generates $\{a^nb^n\}$, which is not regular.
- $\{a^nb^nc^n\}$ is not context-free; the CFG pumping lemma proves it.
- A grammar is **ambiguous** if a string has two parse trees.
- Ambiguity is a property of the grammar, not usually of the language, but inherently ambiguous languages exist.
- Testing an arbitrary grammar for ambiguity is undecidable.
- **Chomsky Normal Form**: every rule is $A \to BC$ or $A \to a$.
- Programming language syntax is context-free, which is why parsers use a stack.
